note: Curated daily by the scheduled ingest. Items are media and public reporting, not programme data. Figures quoted here do not feed the dashboard headlines unless they are also ingested into master_data.csv from a programme source.

items.headline: Namibia's outbreak reaches 17 farms and 129 positive samples in ||Kharas.
items.summary: As at 6 October, 17 farms in the Karasburg district were confirmed infected, up from 15 farms and 127 cases reported on 7 October. Twenty inspection teams have visited 72 of 81 farms within 50 kilometres of the index farm, and 16 veterinary checkpoints are operating. Regional context only, not South African programme data.

items.headline: Dairy farmers at the Royal Show warn that foot and mouth disease may become endemic without better surveillance.
items.summary: FMD Response SA spokesperson Andrew Morphew called for a published national surveillance plan and more testing capacity beyond the single ARC laboratory, and for the state to measure population immunity rather than doses administered. One dairy farmer reported an outbreak affecting 100 vaccinated cows at a cost of about R960,000, against a vaccination cost of about R47 a cow twice a year.

items.headline: Namibia's agriculture minister visits the ||Kharas outbreak area as vaccination teams gather in Karasburg.
items.summary: Minister Inge Zaamwani spent two days in the Karasburg district checking roadblocks and fence construction, and said talks with affected farmers were nearly complete. Most vaccination teams had reached the Karasburg camp, with vaccination to start once schedules are agreed; this differs from earlier reports that vaccination was already under way.

items.headline: Namibia confirms foot and mouth disease in the Zambezi region as the ||Kharas outbreak reaches 17 farms.
items.summary: All 12 samples from cattle at Kalala Island in the Kabbe constituency tested positive on 7 October, and Namibia has suspended movement of cloven-hoofed animals, auctions and local slaughter across the Zambezi region. Emergency vaccination has started there. This is regional context and does not affect our master.

items.headline: Namibia starts building a veterinary cordon fence along the Orange River border.
items.summary: Construction has started on the fence from Homerevier to Velloorsdrift and is expected to take four months, while a proposed 290 kilometre fence from Ariamsvlei to Ai-Ais is costed at about N$47 million. This updates the 7 October item on Namibia's border fencing plan.

items.headline: Meatco places about 400 production workers on paid leave as Namibia's exports stay suspended.
items.summary: Namibia's main beef exporter has sent about 400 of its more than 700 staff on three weeks of special leave with full pay from 1 to 23 October, when it will review the position. It had paid producers about N$31 million for cattle delivered between 29 August and 11 September. No new case count was given.

items.headline: Namibia says its ||Kharas response is on track as work on a containment zone fence begins.
items.summary: As at 6 October, 129 samples had tested positive on 17 farms, with 20 teams inspecting farms within 50 kilometres of the index farm and roadblocks operating day and night. The Orange River cordon fence is expected to take four months, construction of the containment zone fence was due to start in the week of 12 October, and vaccination teams were preparing to deploy. No new case count since 6 October.

items.headline: Foot and mouth disease confirmed in kudu in the Addo Elephant National Park.
items.summary: Wildlife health monitoring picked up more lameness among kudu; a first round of tests was negative, but a second round, run with the Eastern Cape Department of Agriculture, confirmed infection. No other species shows signs, cloven-hoofed animals may not enter or leave the park without veterinary approval, and the park stays open with vehicle disinfection. The source and any link to the Eastern Cape livestock outbreaks are still under investigation; no wildlife figures are held in our master.

items.headline: Meatco proposes paying staff two-thirds of their salaries for three months.
items.summary: Namibia's Meat Corporation has proposed reduced pay from November 2026 to January 2027 as foot and mouth disease restrictions strain its finances. It reports revenue down by N$757 million in 2025/26 and plans a voluntary separation programme. This follows the paid leave for about 400 workers reported on 12 October.

items.headline: Namibian farmers seek supervised movement of livestock to abattoirs while auctions stay closed.
items.summary: The Namibia Agricultural Union plans to ask its veterinary authorities to allow supervised movement of animals to abattoirs, warning that formal approval of new trade protocols could take six to seven months. The RPO says some of our abattoirs struggle to source sheep without Namibian supply, with weaner calf prices at about R57 to R60 a kilogram; it cites Namibian lambs at about 15 percent of our sheep slaughter so far this year, although the article also quotes a figure of more than 70 percent for the abattoirs that depend on them.

items.headline: Namibian farmers seek interim trade arrangements after informal talks with a South African delegation.
items.summary: Namibian farmers' bodies want supervised livestock trade from areas unaffected by the outbreak, warning that a six to seven month halt would threaten farm viability. A South African delegation from the RPO, AgriSA and RMIS shared our experience of permits and traceability; no agreements were reached, and any arrangement needs both countries' veterinary authorities.

items.headline: Namibia's two outbreaks and the European Union restrictions are set out in an international overview.
items.summary: The report brings together the ||Kharas figures (129 positive samples on 17 farms and 72 of 81 targeted farms inspected as at 6 October) and the separate Zambezi outbreak, which officials say is not shown to be directly linked to ||Kharas. It notes that the EU measure covers the former free zone rather than all Namibian meat, and that the Namibia Agricultural Union expects prices to stay under pressure until export markets reopen.

items.headline: The ARC says a funding gap is holding up its planned vaccine manufacturing facility.
items.summary: The Portfolio Committee on Agriculture heard on 6 October that the ARC has received about R535.5 million from Treasury for the facility and spent R81.7 million, but the estimated cost has risen to about R1.6 billion and construction has not started. The article also reports that the Auditor-General could not confirm value for money on R311 million the Department spent on 3.42 million imported doses, and that OBP sold about 17.5 million doses in the year. These are media reports of the committee meeting; our economic boxes and supply pipeline are unchanged pending the primary documents.

items.headline: Roadblocks around the Karasburg outbreak could stay in place until 23 December.
items.summary: Namibian veterinary officials and police have set up fixed and occasional roadblocks around the 17 farms near the index farm, including the Warmbad and Velloorsdrift areas on our border. A local farmer says his small stock exports to South Africa have stopped and lambs could lose N$20 to N$30 a kilogram in value if sales are delayed.

items.headline: Namibia starts compulsory vaccination in Karasburg as its outbreak reaches 18 farms.
items.summary: Vaccination by state officials began on 14 October in three rounds over three months; as at that date 131 animals had tested positive for SAT1 on 18 farms, from 63,011 inspected. In the Zambezi region more than 10,000 cattle have been vaccinated, no new clinical cases were found by 13 October, and officials report no link between the two outbreaks.

items.headline: Daily Dispatch adds detail on the Addo kudu cases and vaccination around the park.
items.summary: Two lame kudu sampled on 1 September tested positive and a warthog tested negative; SANParks says wildlife became infected through exposure to infected livestock, though the source is not confirmed. The report cites 418,176 farm animals vaccinated in the Sarah Baartman and Nelson Mandela Bay areas, a district figure we do not hold in the master, and the RPO says enough vaccine is available through RMIS.

items.headline: GroundUp reports Limpopo's vaccination drive has passed one million doses.
items.summary: Reporting from a booster session near the Kruger National Park, GroundUp says vaccination has reached every Limpopo district, with over one million doses given and about 75 percent of cattle first-vaccinated, and that pigs, goats and sheep are next. It cites 98 confirmed commercial farms under quarantine and 66 suspected to 11 October; these exceed the 971,866 animals (Ministry, 14 September) and 101 positive cases (136 including closed) in our master, which still awaits a newer Limpopo pack.

items.headline: Farmer's Weekly says 1,501 outbreaks remain open although FMD has left the headlines.
items.summary: Drawing on the Department's outbreak report of 30 September, Farmer's Weekly sets out 2,871 outbreaks nationally, 1,370 closed and 1,501 open, with the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal holding about half of the open outbreaks. It also traces how the SAT1 and SAT2 strains spread between provinces. These figures match the WOAH report rows already in our master (ingested 11 October), so nothing new was added.

items.headline: Namibia says its outbreak remains confined to the Karasburg district.
items.summary: Veterinary Public Notification No. 20 of 2026 reports 131 animals positive on 18 farms as at 15 October, all in the Karasburg district, with SAT1 confirmed. Movement north of the veterinary cordon fence remains permitted except in the Zambezi region, and animals in registered feedlots or quarantine may go to registered abattoirs only after 30 days without new intake and negative tests.

items.headline: Zambezi households lose income as auctions and slaughter stay suspended.
items.summary: The Namibian reports the human cost of the Zambezi restrictions, where auctions, movement and slaughter are suspended after 12 cattle samples tested positive at Kalala Island. Namibia's ministry says the two outbreaks are not linked and that it will vaccinate rather than cull; the Namibia Agricultural Union notes the region has long been classed as FMD-infected.

items.headline: Namibian economists warn the outbreak threatens the expected livestock recovery and export earnings.
items.summary: The Economic Association of Namibia says the outbreak puts at risk livestock growth the central bank had forecast at 2.2 percent for 2026 and 4.6 percent for 2027. It cites 131 positive animals on 18 farms after inspection of 63,011 animals as at 14 October, and calls for trade negotiations and financial relief.

items.headline: Namibia's chief veterinary officer confirms 131 cases on 18 farms as surveillance is stepped up.
items.summary: Dr Kennedy Shoombe says the ||Kharas outbreak still stands at 131 cases on 18 farms, unchanged since 14 October, with movement controls in the Karasburg veterinary district to be tightened under Public Veterinary Notice No. 20 of 2026. The Namibia Chamber of Commerce and Industry gave N$1.5 million to the national FMD support fund.

items.headline: Namibia revisits plans for its own foot and mouth vaccine plant.
items.summary: Namibia imports most of its FMD vaccine from the Botswana Vaccine Institute under a fixed three-year supply agreement. A 2015 plan for a vaccine plant at Eenhana never became a working facility, and the outbreak has renewed calls for local production.

items.headline: South African and Namibian industry bodies set out positions on future livestock trade protocols.
items.summary: Following the industry talks between the RMIS, RPO and AgriSA and Namibian producer bodies, RMIS calls for separate protocols for sheep and cattle, with no shortcuts for cattle, which would need to come from below the ||Kharas red zone, be vaccinated and spend at least two weeks in a feedlot. RMIS stresses that the veterinary authorities of the two countries must set the final protocols; between 80 and 90 percent of Namibian sheep are destined for our market.

items.headline: South African feedlots will not support cattle and beef imports from Namibia and Botswana for now.
items.summary: The South African Feedlot Association's executive committee unanimously decided not to support imports of live cattle and beef from Namibia and Botswana while foot and mouth disease remains a concern, to protect our export markets. It acknowledges the local calf shortage and says it will review the position later.

items.headline: Daily Maverick says foot and mouth disease at Addo may affect up to a tenth of the park's kudu.
items.summary: The SANParks veterinarian estimates that 5 to 10 percent of the kudu in Addo Elephant National Park are probably infected, and red hartebeest and eland have also shown clinical signs. The park may have to stay out of the annual Kirkwood game auction, where its buffalo bulls earned R1.28 million last year. These wildlife cases are not in our programme figures.

items.headline: Concern grows over foot and mouth disease in kudu at Addo Elephant National Park.
items.summary: Two kudu sampled on 1 September tested positive and SANParks confirmed the infection on 13 October; between 5 and 10 percent of the park's kudu show lameness, and red hartebeest and eland show signs that are not yet confirmed. The park is under quarantine and SANParks says transmission to its buffalo cannot be ruled out. The Eastern Cape reports 418,176 animals vaccinated in Sarah Baartman and Nelson Mandela Bay.

items.headline: Namibia vaccinates 1,296 cattle in Karasburg and more than 42,000 in Zambezi.
items.summary: In its weekly update the Namibian agriculture ministry said compulsory vaccination in the Karasburg veterinary district had reached 1,296 cattle on 25 farms by 21 October, out of about 13,000 targeted in the first round, with 19 teams deployed. In the Zambezi region 42,286 cattle have been vaccinated at 34 crush pens and no new cases have been found outside the disease management area.

items.headline: Media report the medium-term budget sets aside R606 million for foot and mouth disease.
items.summary: IOL reports that the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement of 21 October gives the Department of Agriculture R606 million to contain the disease: R423.4 million reprioritised within the Department in 2026/27 and R183 million rolled over for vaccines. This compares with the R1.3 billion the Department asked for in September. We have not yet seen the Treasury document, so our economic impact box is unchanged.

items.headline: Namibia's mid-year budget proposes N$179 million to contain foot and mouth disease.
items.summary: Namibia's mid-year budget review proposes N$179 million for containing the outbreak, close to the N$190 million the agriculture ministry estimated in early October. No compensation scheme was announced for farmers' losses from delayed sales and movement restrictions.

items.headline: Farmer's Weekly says the budget offers farmers some relief, including R183 million carried forward for vaccines.
items.summary: Farmer's Weekly reports that the Adjusted Estimates of National Expenditure carry forward R183 million for foot and mouth disease vaccine procurement, which our CEO Johann Kotze welcomed while calling for a sustained, properly funded vaccination and biosecurity programme. TLU SA noted that the budget statement made no new specific allocation for disease control. This is a media report; our state spending box is unchanged until we see the Treasury document.

items.headline: Four men are arrested in Namibia for allegedly breaking foot and mouth disease rules.
items.summary: Republikein reports that four men, including a farmer, were arrested over the weekend for allegedly transporting raw meat in breach of the movement regulations. Enforcement of the controls around the outbreak area continues.

items.headline: Namibia declares the whole ||Kharas region a foot and mouth disease control area as farmers warn of job losses.
items.summary: At an information session in Keetmanshoop, veterinary officials said all movement of live cloven-hoofed animals into, out of and within ||Kharas is suspended, and that the region will be split into smaller containment zones using game fences. Farmers and the Namibia Agricultural Union are asking for supervised movement from unaffected farms and bio-secure transit routes; officials could not say when these might be approved.

items.headline: A Namibian legal analysis sets out the trade and compliance implications of the outbreak for farmers.
items.summary: A Cliffe Dekker Hofmeyr partner notes that exports to South Africa, the European Union, China and the United States have stopped, and that government estimates N$190.2 million for containment, including about N$47 million for 290 kilometres of control fencing. He urges farmers to report suspected cases, keep traceability records and document their losses. This is an opinion piece; our Namibia headline figures use the N$179 million in the mid-year budget.

items.headline: Namibia vaccinates more than 50,000 cattle in Zambezi as the minister visits the outbreak area.
items.summary: Agriculture Minister Inge Zaamwani visited the Zambezi region, where more than 50,000 cattle were vaccinated over two weeks to build a buffer zone. New Era reports more than 1,300 cattle affected at 18 crush pens across Kabbe South, Kabbe North, Katima Rural and Kongola, and checkpoint staff raised shortages of staff and supplies. Regional context only; it does not change any South African figure.

items.headline: Meatco runs a two-day slaughter of its own feedlot cattle for the Namibian domestic market only.
items.summary: Meatco slaughtered cattle already in its feedlots on 27 and 28 October under the veterinary standard operating procedure, with all beef sold locally at prices well below export levels. Normal slaughter has been suspended since 23 September, and any wider restart depends on further veterinary directives. Export markets remain closed.

items.headline: Namibia's livestock board expects a weaker final quarter after the outbreak disrupted September marketing.
items.summary: The Livestock and Livestock Products Board reports year-to-date cattle marketing up 30.9 percent to 217,007 head, but September marketing fell 27.2 percent as movement controls took hold. South Africa took 46.9 percent of Namibia's lamb and mutton exports and 78,746 live goats went to our feedlots, flows now halted. Some pork figures in the article are internally inconsistent.

items.headline: Namibia reports no new foot and mouth cases and more than 61,000 cattle vaccinated in both regions.
items.summary: The Namibian agriculture ministry says no new cases were found in ||Kharas or Zambezi by 28 October. In ||Kharas 7,402 cattle on 81 farms have been vaccinated (131 cases on 18 farms, unchanged), and in Zambezi 53,913 cattle at 37 crush pens, where about 1,300 cases are reported at 18 crush pens on Kalala Island. A second surveillance round has started in ||Kharas and exports of animals from outside ||Kharas may proceed subject to destination requirements.

items.headline: Our first joint quarterly trade report with Agbiz shows a US$2.14 billion agricultural trade surplus as foot and mouth disease keeps key red meat markets closed.
items.summary: The AgriSA and Agbiz quarterly agricultural trade report puts second-quarter 2026 exports at US$4.12 billion and the surplus at US$2.14 billion, with livestock exports up 27.9 percent on the first quarter as the red meat industry works around closed markets. Our chief executive Johann Kotzé named foot and mouth disease, port and rail performance and phytosanitary access as the constraints within our control. This is trade context, not programme data.

items.headline: Meatco cuts cattle producer prices by about 20 percent from 1 November as export markets stay closed.
items.summary: Namibia's Meat Corporation has lowered its cattle producer prices by about 20 percent for November, so farmers receive nearly N$15 less per kilogram; the average price for carcasses of 220 kilograms and above falls from N$75.08 to N$60.17 per kilogram. Meatco says its earlier prices were not sustainable while slaughter is limited to the lower-priced domestic market, and it is pursuing markets in Africa and the Middle East.

items.headline: About 240 jobs at Namibia's Savanna Beef export abattoir are at risk after the outbreak halted operations.
items.summary: Savanna Beef Processors stopped slaughtering after foot and mouth disease was found in Namibia's free zone on 23 September; before the outbreak it had reached 250 head a day and exported about 100 containers of beef to the United Kingdom, the European Union and Norway. Management hopes limited slaughtering may resume towards the end of November. The Beef Value Chain Forum has approved N$500,000 for an international expert to help Namibia regain its veterinary status.

items.headline: Namibian beef shipped to the United Kingdom after the ban must be returned or sent to other markets.
items.summary: Namibia's chief veterinary officer said beef had to enter the United Kingdom before 25 September, so containers still at sea when the ban took effect must come back or be redirected. He said market access negotiations have started with trading partners and that talks with Mauritius have been concluded after Namibia showed the outbreak is confined.

items.headline: The Bank of Namibia orders banks to offer repayment holidays and restructuring to farmers hit by the outbreak and drought.
items.summary: Directive BID-42, enacted on 30 October, lets commercial banks grant loan repayment holidays of 1 to 24 months, restructure loans and extend new credit to livestock, crop and wildlife farmers and dependent businesses affected by foot and mouth disease or El Nino conditions. Clients granted relief stay classed as performing with credit bureaus, and banks must give written reasons if they decline an application.

items.headline: Namibia plans a double fence and a WOAH-recognised containment zone in ||Kharas that would last two years.
items.summary: Speaking on 30 October, Namibia's chief veterinary officer said the government will build a double disease control fence in ||Kharas to separate infected farms and then apply to WOAH for a containment zone valid for two years, so that trade can resume from areas outside it. Namibia aims to regain freedom without vaccination; industry leaders said farmers inside the zone face a longer recovery but will stay part of market negotiations.

items.headline: Namibia sets out which meat and milk products may move under its foot and mouth disease rules.
items.summary: Pasteurised milk, commercially cooked meat, biltong and droewors from registered facilities may move countrywide, but raw meat may not cross the veterinary cordon fence southwards or leave ||Kharas while controls continue. Imports of raw meat and cloven-hoofed animal products from South Africa and Botswana remain banned without veterinary permits and health certificates.

items.headline: Namibian farmers put foot and mouth disease losses at N$13 million a day as markets stay closed.
items.summary: At the Bank Windhoek Agricultural Series on 30 October the Namibia Agricultural Union estimated value chain losses of N$2.4 billion over six months and some 52,000 jobs at risk south of the cordon fence. The chief veterinary officer reported 131 positive samples on 18 farms in ||Kharas as at 27 October, 8,102 of 13,000 cattle vaccinated there and 53,913 of 56,360 in Zambezi, 1,344 cattle through controlled slaughter, and talks with Tunisia, Morocco and Nigeria; the ||Kharas vaccination figure is higher than the 7,402 the ministry gave for 28 October.

items.headline: Namibia may review its foot and mouth disease restrictions before the festive season if no new cases appear.
items.summary: The chief veterinary officer said that by 4 November surveillance had found no case outside the two outbreak areas, and restrictions could be reviewed before December if that holds. The ministry still reports 131 cases on 18 farms in ||Kharas, with 51 farms inspected in the second surveillance round and 19 roadblocks and checkpoints across ||Kharas, Hardap, Khomas and Otjozondjupa.

items.headline: Namibia's industry-led foot and mouth disease support fund reaches about N$16.2 million.
items.summary: The FMD Support Fund, set up by Namibia's four farmers' unions, has raised about N$16.2 million in donations and pledges, including N$1.6 million from B2Gold Namibia, towards a first-phase target of N$50 million. It buys equipment and supplies requested by the veterinary services for field teams, checkpoints and fence repairs; New Era put the total at more than N$15.35 million.

items.headline: RMIS confirms a new four-year red meat statutory levy cycle to 2030.
items.summary: The new levy cycle, published in Government Gazette No. 55673, runs to 4 November 2030 at R15.80 a head of cattle and R3.08 a head of small stock for 2026/27, with RMIS as administrator. RMIS says the levy funded its Disease Operations Centre, set up in under 90 days during the outbreak, vaccines secured for industry at cost price and the tagging campaign; its national traceability platform now has more than 15,000 registered production units.

items.headline: Namibia's finance minister confirms N$179 million for foot and mouth containment in the mid-year budget debate.
items.summary: Finance Minister Ericah Shafudah told Parliament that N$179 million has been allocated to contain the outbreak, which threatens beef access to the European Union and the United Kingdom. A further N$685 million reallocated from non-performing projects will partly fund foot and mouth containment alongside grain reserves, medical aid and the contingency fund; the share for foot and mouth was not stated.

items.headline: Namibia says its ||Kharas outbreak is contained, with 8,267 cattle vaccinated on 90 farms.
items.summary: Namibia's agriculture ministry says the Karasburg outbreak remains confined to that district, with 18 farms and 131 positive cases as at 4 November. Compulsory vaccination has now reached 8,267 cattle on 90 farms, up from the 7,402 on 81 farms the ministry gave for 28 October, and 53,913 cattle have been vaccinated in Zambezi with no new cases outside its disease management area. This is regional context and does not affect any figure in our master.

items.headline: No new foot and mouth cases in the Free State as the provincial outbreak nears its end.
items.summary: Reports the Free State department's release of 6 November: no new cases in the past week, the cumulative count unchanged at 804, with 799 resolved and 5 still under quarantine. The same release puts cattle vaccinated at 1,762,772, which we have ingested from the department's own statistics; the media report adds no new figures.

items.headline: Foot and mouth disease reshapes livestock shows, with a national protocol now in place.
items.summary: The Bloem Show chief executive told the Commonwealth Agricultural Conference in Cape Town that South African shows were closed to cattle, sheep, goats and pigs for the first six months of the year. Requirements for livestock entering shows grew from three to eight, including compulsory vaccination, a booster 21 days before transport, quarantine, veterinary sign-off and traceability, under one national protocol set by the new South African Show Association.

items.headline: Namibia's economic task force calls for an urgent livestock trade deal with South Africa.
items.summary: The Presidential Task Force on Economic Recovery and Transformation wants Namibia to negotiate a bilateral arrangement with South Africa so that exports of weaners, sheep, goats and meat can resume. It says the domestic market absorbs only 30 to 40 percent of Namibian meat. This is regional context and does not affect any figure in our master.

items.headline: Namibia's livestock board puts lost sales at close to N$1 billion in six weeks.
items.summary: An opinion piece cites the Livestock and Livestock Products Board's estimate of about N$150 million a week in lost livestock sales since the outbreak was confirmed on 23 September. It notes that regaining WOAH status will not by itself reopen markets, because South Africa, the European Union, Norway and China will each set their own conditions.

items.headline: Meatco weighs recalling about 96 tonnes of beef held in South Africa.
items.summary: Four or five containers of Meatco beef that entered South Africa before the outbreak cannot be exported without fresh certification, and Meatco may bring them home or sell them here. The report repeats RPO figures of 417,808 lambs and 36,821 weaner calves imported from Namibia so far in 2026, and notes that some of our abattoirs rely on Namibia for more than 70 percent of their sheep.

items.headline: Namibia looks to regional markets as its export suspensions continue.
items.summary: The Livestock and Livestock Products Board is negotiating with regional markets that can accept Namibia's current status, while farmers in Rehoboth describe mounting feed and finance costs with no outlet for their animals. The report puts total Namibian FMD vaccinations at 62,180 cattle, consistent with 8,267 in ||Kharas and 53,913 in Zambezi.

items.headline: Namibia prepares a first meat container for Zambia and plans a staged return to South African trade.
items.summary: The livestock board says a container will go to Zambia soon and that the first six months of its trade recovery plan focus on reopening trade with South Africa and other neighbours. It warns the local market could be flooded if exports stay closed; some sheep producers are already sending animals to approved abattoirs.

items.headline: Namibia completes its first vaccination round in ||Kharas with no new cases for three weeks.
items.summary: The ministry's update of 11 November says the first round in ||Kharas is complete, with the 13,000 targeted cattle nearly all vaccinated, and cases unchanged at 131 on 18 farms. Risk-based surveillance will now extend south of the Veterinary Cordon Fence, including communal areas, and a booster round is planned for Kalala Island in Zambezi, where no case has been found outside the management area for three weeks.

items.headline: Meatco suspends slaughter as export closures strain its finances.
items.summary: Meatco says more than 85 percent of its earnings came from exports suspended since 23 September and that it has suspended slaughter until it can resume sustainably. It is consulting the union on cost measures for nearly 800 staff, with a monthly wage bill of about N$15 million.
